# odin-http: where this copy comes from

The starter's HTTP server is a fork of [laytan/odin-http](https://github.com/laytan/odin-http) (MIT, `LICENSE`),
vendored in-tree so that its changes live next to the code that needs them (D11; ANSWERS F3). There is no separate
fork repo: an upstream offer goes through a GitHub fork made at that time from the changes listed below (PLAN §8.1).

- **Base:** `fac113fbd828aad3d71479a534b5de4358b6a07b` (2026-08-26, "openssl: update bundled libraries to
  openssl-3.6.4 (#120)"), the commit the skeleton pinned as its `app/odin-http` submodule. Upstream had no newer
  commit when this was vendored (2026-10-26).
- **What is vendored:** only the `http` package's own files, `LICENSE` and `README.md`. Left out: `client/`,
  `comparisons/`, `docs/`, `examples/`, `old_nbio/`, `openssl/`, `.editorconfig` and `odinfmt.json`. The server path
  uses `core:nbio` and needs no OpenSSL.
- **Odin:** `dev-2026-10` (`84bc3fc`), the toolchain pin of the Dockerfile and CI.

## Local changes

Each change is generic (nothing starter-specific goes in here), keeps upstream's style, and is listed with the files
it touches. The WS codec, the SSE encoder, the multipart writer, Range parsing and the hub stay in the starter's
`platform/stream` and `platform/hub` (PLAN §8.1), so this diff stays small enough to offer upstream.

| # | Change | Files | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| F-1 | Streams: a `Streaming` connection state, `Connection.stream`, and `stream.odin` (`stream_begin`, `stream_write`, `stream_end` with an optional deadline, `stream_queued`, `stream_would_overflow`, `stream_loop`, `on_data`, `on_close`, `on_shutdown`); chunked, raw (after a 101) and close-delimited bodies; a send queue capped at 256 KiB (`Too_Slow`), and an end with a deadline so a protocol can send a slow consumer a last message (WebSocket 1013) and still cut it off | `stream.odin`, `server.odin` | M0 spike (S0.2, S0.3) |
| F-2 | HTTP/1.0 peers get a close-delimited stream body instead of chunked | `stream.odin` | M0 spike |
| F-3 | `stream_sendfile` on `nbio.sendfile`, for Range responses | — | planned (M9's video) |
| F-4 | `Server_Opts.on_thread_init` and `on_thread_shutdown`, with each thread's index; M2 (M1-05): `on_thread_release`, at the end of a thread's shutdown just before it releases its event loop, where the application stops other threads posting to it | `server.odin` | M0 spike (S0.6, S0.7) |
| F-5 | `Server_Opts.invoke`: accept, the scanner's reads (and the handler dispatch inside them), response sends and stream callbacks run through it; when it reports a crash, the connection answers 500 if nothing was sent and closes, and a stream gets `on_crash` and ends (`Stream_End.Crashed`) | `server.odin`, `scanner.odin`, `response.odin`, `stream.odin` | M0 spike (S0.2, S0.6) |
| F-6 | `Content-Length` must be plain digits within `int` (`parse_content_length`); anything else answers 400, so `-5` no longer reaches `assert(n >= 0)` in the scanner, `OPTIONS *` included | `body.odin` | M0 spike (S0.2, S0.6) |
| F-7 | Timeouts on the scanner's reads: idle 75 s, headers 10 s from a request's first byte, body 30 s (`idle_timeout`, `header_timeout`, `body_timeout`; 0 = none), enforced by one 1 s sweep per thread over its connections' deadlines, not a timeout on every read (on io_uring that is a linked operation per request, which cost 2–4 % on the lightest route, S0.2); a timed-out peer reads as EOF, and a body cut off part way closes the connection after its 400. M2 (M1-02): `send_timeout` (30 s) bounds one send, a response's or a stream's: the sweep cuts a connection whose send is still in flight past it, as the drain cuts one (`shutdown`), so a client that never reads can't hold its descriptor and a copy of its response forever | `scanner.odin`, `server.odin`, `response.odin`, `stream.odin` | M0 spike (S0.2, S0.7); the drills' `slowread` |
| F-8 | `max_connections` (default: the open-file soft limit − 64 on Linux and macOS, none on Windows) answers 503 past the cap; an accept error is logged and the accept re-posted instead of `panicf` | `server.odin`, `limits_posix.odin`, `limits_windows.odin` | M0 spike (S0.2, S0.7) |
| F-9 | Bounded shutdown: the accept stops at once, idle connections and those still reading their headers close with their read cancelled, streams get 2 s, active requests `drain_deadline` (5 s) before their sockets are cut (past it, closing connections no longer hold the loop), and leftover operations 500 ms | `server.odin` | M0 spike (S0.7: 5.6 s with 500 SSE + 500 WS + a slowloris + a half body + an idle peer) |
| F-10 | SIGTERM as well as SIGINT; the second-signal check is a process-wide flag (upstream read a thread-local that is nil on a thread that isn't the server's); `server_is_closing` | `server.odin` | M0 spike (S0.7) |
| F-11 | The `date` header is formatted per thread, once per second of its loop's clock, instead of in one shared buffer a timer rewrote under the readers | `server.odin` | M0 spike (S0.2) |
| F-12 | `listen` logs an error naming io_uring and seccomp when the event loop can't start, instead of asserting, and retries a bind that fails with `Address_In_Use` for `bind_retry` (3 s) | `server.odin` | M0 spike (S0.7) |
| F-13 | Deferred responses: `response_defer` hands out a `Response_Ref` (loop, socket, a per-thread request generation) and `response_resume` returns the Response on that loop, or nil once the connection is gone or has moved on; while deferred, a poll on the socket closes the connection when the peer leaves and calls the application's `on_gone`; a thread's shutdown waits (to `drain_deadline`) for the refs it still owes. M2 (M1-04): `response_crashed` answers 500 and closes for a continuation that crashed after `response_resume`, as `connection_crashed` does on the fork's own paths; a connection whose 500 is queued ignores a second crash, which closed it under that send (M2-12), and that send has a deadline like any other (M2-28) | `deferred.odin`, `server.odin`, `response.odin` | M0 spike (S0.5) |
| F-14 | The chunked body decoder refuses bad input instead of asserting: chunk data not followed by CRLF answers 400 (upstream asserted), trailer fields are discarded, at most 32 lines (upstream parsed them into the request's read-only headers, which asserted), and a chunk size is 1–15 plain hex digits (strconv took a sign and `_` and wrapped past 64 bits). Found by the M1 audit (`docs/audit/M1.md`, M1-01): one client could stop the process with about 101 such requests a minute | `body.odin` | M1 audit |
| F-15 | Throughput on the response path, from a profile of the write path behind M1's parity gate: header values are written whole (or in spans around a newline) instead of rune by rune through a stream (12 % of a write's CPU); a lookup with a key that is already lower case skips `sanitize_key`'s copy, which copies byte by byte now; and F-13's watch is optional (`response_defer(…, watch)`), since its two extra operations per deferred reply cost 7 % where the reply is due within milliseconds | `http.odin`, `response.odin`, `headers.odin`, `deferred.odin` | M1 parity gate |
| F-16 | The re-read of M1-17..M1-22 (`docs/audit/M1.md`): a scan asked for from inside a scan callback is queued and run by the outermost `scanner_scan` once the callback returns (upstream nested one call per buffered token, and 12,000 one-byte chunks overflowed a Windows loop's stack, a pure crash the burst rule turns into an exit); chunk framing counts against the body cap (at least 4 KiB), chunk-size lines, line ends and trailer lines are at most 4 KiB (bounded in the split functions, since the scanner's `max_token_size` is checked only when its buffer grows) and the first two end in CRLF only, whitespace may come only before a `;`, leading zeros don't count toward a size's 15 digits, and a scan error in the trailers is an error, not the end of the body; a 64-bit `int` is asserted; a client's malformed request or reset logs at info, not warn or error, and a drain refused after the handler answered logs the status it sends; `response_defer` doesn't watch beside a body read the trampoline has queued; the upstream test `test_dynamic_unwritten` frees what it makes, so the fork runs under the unit tests | `scanner.odin`, `body.odin`, `server.odin`, `response.odin`, `http.odin`, `body_test.odin` | M1 audit (re-read) |
| F-17 | An open stream holds little: its receive buffer is sized by kind (64 B for a chunked stream, which reads only to notice the peer leaving; 2 KiB for a raw one), `stream_begin` gives the scanner's buffer back, and once the handler returns with a stream the connection's arena goes back too, zeroed so its first block is mapped only on use (for a handler called from the headers where it returns, and for one called from a body's callback, a POST stream, where that callback returns: `_body_returned`, M2-21 in M3); `on_data` runs on the thread's temp allocator. An idle SSE stream held about 16 KiB before, 3.0 KiB after (WS 5.0; Linux, 4000 held; `docs/perf/STREAMS.md`) | `stream.odin`, `server.odin` | M2 stream budgets |
| F-18 | A request that follows a chunked stream on its connection is read whole. The stream's read (kept to notice the peer leaving) could take the start of the next request, which a keep-alive client sends the moment the last chunk lands, and dropped it, and `nbio.remove` drops the bytes of a read that had already completed: the scanner then read the request from its middle (a 501) or waited for one already gone (k6 at 20 VUs: 0.01-0.1 % of the requests after a stream; a raw socket, about 1 in 300). Now a chunked stream keeps what it reads and reads no further, and a stream that ends with a read still in flight parks until that read returns, then hands every byte to the scanner; a parked stream waits no longer than an idle connection would, and shutdown or a crash closes it. A crash in the request served after the hand-over is that connection's (500, close), not the stream's | `stream.odin` | M2, lab's keep-alive protocol check |
| F-19 | Windows: an accepted socket takes the listener's context. core:nbio sets `SO_UPDATE_ACCEPT_CONTEXT` after `AcceptEx` with no value, which Windows rejects, so `shutdown()` on every accepted socket failed (`Invalid_Argument`): F-9's drain cut and F-7's send cut did nothing. The fork repeats the call with the listening socket after each accept (upstream-worthy for core:nbio) | `accept_windows.odin`, `accept_posix.odin`, `server.odin` | M2, the drills' `slowread` |
| F-20 | The request's and the response's header maps are reserved up front (16 each), so the usual headers fit without the map regrowing (3.7 regrowths a request in M1's profile; about +1.5 % on `write` and `pages`, Windows) | `headers.odin`, `request.odin`, `response.odin` | M2, M1's profile follow-up |
| F-21 | `server_shutdown` never wakes a released loop or reads freed threads. It runs on another thread (maybe in a signal handler, so it takes no lock) while each loop shuts itself down: upstream woke loops that had already been released (a write to a freed, maybe reused, eventfd) and copied each `Server_Thread` while its loop wrote it, and `serve` could free `threads` under the wake loop. A count of calls in progress, which a loop about to release and `serve` about to free wait out, and a `released` flag the call checks. Found by ThreadSanitizer (M2's gate) | `server.odin` | M2 TSan gate |
| F-22 | Under `-sanitize:thread` a connection's arena is the runtime's heap-backed one (`Conn_Arena`): ThreadSanitizer doesn't see core:mem/virtual's raw `mmap`/`munmap` syscalls, so pages one loop unmapped and another mapped again read as a race on every reuse (about a hundred reports a run, none real); `malloc`/`free` it sees, and a real use after free stays reportable. Other builds keep `virtual.Arena` | `server.odin`, `response.odin`, `scanner.odin` | M2 TSan gate |
| F-23 | A serving loop's tick doesn't wait on the kernel while callbacks have queued work for the loop (`_server_tick`). core:nbio's Linux tick (io_uring) runs only what was queued before it began and then waits with no timeout, so a next_tick or a 0 ms timeout queued from a callback waited for some unrelated event: on a quiet loop the next 1 s timer, about 460 ms per word for the bot's mock at `BOT_DELAY_MS=0`, which failed CI's k6 run. Its Windows and posix ticks already pass 0 then; the test `queued_work_runs_without_waiting` (50 next ticks beside a 100 ms timer) took 4.9 s on Linux before, 1 ms after. A core:nbio fix, to report upstream | `server.odin`, `server_test.odin` | M2, CI's k6 coverage |
| F-24 | A HEAD's answer is the GET's heading without its body. Upstream runs a HEAD as a GET (`redirect_head_to_get`, on by default) and meant to send it as a HEAD, but set the method on a copy of the request line, so the whole body went out; on a keep-alive connection a client then reads that body as the start of the next response (the stack Caddy logged "Unsolicited response received on idle HTTP channel"). `_response_write_heading` records where the body starts, and `response_send_got_body` truncates a HEAD's buffer there; the `Content-Length` stays the GET's, as RFC 9110 §9.3.2 allows. The spec `a HEAD answers headers only` (routing.spec.ts) sends a HEAD and a GET on one connection | `response.odin`, `responses.odin` | M3's stack test |

"M0 spike" means the change is in and the named spikes exercise it (`docs/spikes/`); M1 productionises it with its own
tests (PLAN §22.3). Spike S0.2 measures F-1 and F-5..F-12 under the skeleton's k6 suite before anything builds on them.

## Bumping

1. Copy the new upstream commit's package files over this directory (same list as above), keeping this file.
2. Re-apply the local changes, one commit each, and update the table and the base line above.
3. Re-run the stream contract suite and the parity gate (PLAN §18) before anything ships on the new base.
